title: Post-operative deterioration
subtitle: It is a leak until proven otherwise

sources.title: International guidelines for management of sepsis and septic shock
Guidelines for the management of intra-abdominal infections
Classification of surgical complications: a new proposal with evaluation in a cohort of 6336 patients

red_flags.text: Unexplained tachycardia after an anastomosis. The single most reliable early sign of a leak, and the most frequently explained away.
New atrial fibrillation after abdominal surgery. It is a marker of a septic or ischaemic complication, not a cardiology problem.
Rising oxygen requirement, or a respiratory rate above 20 that nobody has recorded.
Oliguria that does not respond to a fluid challenge.
Pain that increases after day two, or pain that needs more analgesia today than yesterday.
Confusion or agitation in an elderly post-operative patient. Assume sepsis or hypoxia before delirium.
Feculent, bilious or enteric drain output, however small the volume.

do_now.text: See the patient yourself. A deteriorating post-operative patient described over the phone is the classic route to a delayed re-laparotomy.
Full set of observations including respiratory rate, plus a lactate and a venous gas.
If septic, start the sepsis pathway now and hunt the surgical source in parallel rather than afterwards.
Inform the operating surgeon. The person who did the operation knows what is most likely to have failed.

assess.text: Score the deterioration objectively so the escalation is not a matter of opinion.
Work through the differential by day: day 1 to 2 bleeding, atelectasis, cardiac; day 3 to 5 anastomotic leak, chest and urinary infection; day 5 onwards collection, wound, venous thromboembolism.
Examine the wound and every drain personally, and look at the actual output rather than the chart entry.
Review the operation note: what was anastomosed, what was left in, what the surgeon was worried about.
Review the drug chart for missed thromboprophylaxis, omitted usual medication, and analgesia that has been escalating quietly.

investigate.text: FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, lactate, coagulation, blood cultures. CRP from day three onwards is a useful negative predictor for leak.
Contrast CT of the operated compartment. If the question is a leak, the answer is a CT, not another 24 hours of observation.
Chest radiograph and ECG for the respiratory or cardiac presentations; CT pulmonary angiography if embolism is plausible.
Amylase on drain fluid after pancreatic surgery, and bilirubin on drain fluid after biliary surgery.
Urinalysis and culture, and a bladder scan: retention and catheter-associated infection are common and easily missed.

resuscitate.text: Oxygen, fluid to a measured response, and analgesia adequate to allow deep breathing and mobilisation.
Broad-spectrum antimicrobials against the local antibiogram once cultures are taken and a source is suspected.
Correct electrolytes and glucose, restart thromboprophylaxis if it is safe, and stop the drug that is making things worse.
Escalate the level of care while the diagnosis is still uncertain, not after it is confirmed.

definitive.text: Source control: percutaneous drainage of a discrete collection, or re-operation for a leak, ischaemia or uncontrolled contamination.
A negative CT in a patient who continues to deteriorate is not reassurance. Re-image or re-explore.
Where a leak is confirmed, decide early between proximal diversion, repair, or resection with a stoma. Delayed indecision is what kills.
Grade and record the complication consistently so the unit's outcomes mean something.

escalate.text: Consultant surgeon, and critical care, at the point of recognition rather than at the point of certainty.
Interventional radiology for a drainable collection; theatre for anything that will not drain through a tube.
If the patient is not clearly improving within 12 to 24 hours of a plan, the plan is wrong. Change it rather than extend it.

notes: Unexplained tachycardia after an anastomosis is a leak until a CT says otherwise. There is no safer default.
Most delayed re-laparotomies were preceded by 24 hours of somebody being reassured by a normal blood pressure.
The operating surgeon should always be told. Not to apportion blame, but because they hold information no chart contains.
